items.text: When a clue describes a relational trope, search broadly across genres rather than assuming romance-only
When clues include relocation, early writing age, and a degree, prioritize famous authors with documented biographies before niche matches
Always use retrieval tools to locate and read the exact source document before quoting; never answer from background knowledge
When a question specifies source date and publication, treat exact wording as success criterion and verify it verbatim against the passage
When retrieved sources conflict on a key fact, investigate both rather than defaulting to the most familiar source
After locating a candidate publication title in a snippet, re-search the corpus verbatim to verify exact wording before answering
Once a primary entity and its affiliate are confirmed, pivot to a related entity linked by family or professional ties and search their attributes jointly
Before finalizing, verify every distinctive claim against at least one independent source; persist only when multiple clues align
When initial clue matches point to one genre, semantically describe the full combined plot in one query before drilling into specifics
When asked for a specific name, search famous literary characters whose role is replaced by a protagonist in classic novels
For author-biographical clues about a pioneer parent, search the author's own biography and family page before inferring from plot
Fully read all high-relevance semantic search results before drawing conclusions, even when lexical results seem more authoritative
When one regional hypothesis stalls on a key clue, pivot early to alternative regions rather than deepening the same branch
Before committing to a hypothesis, run a sanity-check search for the presumed answer's title or author to falsify the guess
